column4: Mary receives glad tidings of a divinely given child, placing the son's identity inside God's gift and decree before conception rather than inside a human preference for males.
Mary asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer says God creates what He wills; this marks an explicit exception to the section's union-to-birth sequence.
Zechariah names his wife's barrenness while asking God for an heir, making the hoped-for child a gift across a concrete reproductive limit.
The announcement of John answers Zechariah's request with a named boy bestowed through divine glad tidings.
Zechariah asks how a boy is possible with a barren wife and his own extreme age, stating the bodily obstacle that the gift crosses.
God calls this birth easy for Him and recalls Zechariah's prior creation from nothing, locating yusr in divine creative power rather than in the child's male sex.
God's creating, proportioning, and balancing of the human closely joins the section's creation word to its concern with making a body fit.
God composes the human in whatever form He wills, completing 82:7 with divine choice over embodied form rather than a human scale of preferred sex.
Men may neither inherit women against their will nor constrain wives to recover part of what was given them, so marriage-giving cannot become a means of possessing or devaluing the woman.
Women's adornment is to remain covered from the public but may be shown to husbands, giving a legal boundary for the section's scene of bridal disclosure and spousal looking.
Three household privacy times—before dawn prayer, midday undressing, and after night prayer—bring clothing, intimacy, night, and daylight thresholds into one domestic scene.

In the setting of the Prophet's marriage meal, guests must leave and address his wives from behind a screen, a wedding-context boundary to the section's image of a bride being unveiled to her husband.
A wife declared to be like one's mother does not become a mother; mothers are only those who gave birth, sharply distinguishing spousehood and sexual union from maternity.
God cleaves the dawn, makes night for rest, and measures sun and moon, joining the section's dawn disclosure and dark repose to divine determination.
Night for rest and day for seeking divine bounty are paired so people may give thanks, linking the section's cover-and-disclosure cycle with provision and gratitude.
It is generally unlawful to take back anything given to wives at divorce, reinforcing the bridal gift as a protected transfer rather than a temporary price.
Divorced women are owed a fair provision as a duty upon the God-conscious, extending giving beyond union and tying it to taqwā.
Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision are declared lost, connecting rejection of a child with the same refusal of divine gift and provision that the section opposes.
The command not to kill children from poverty is grounded in God's provision for parents and children, opposing economic withholding to the reception of birth as gift.
Abraham's visitors announce a knowledgeable boy, another direct formulation of a son received as divine glad tidings.
Abraham responds that old age has reached him and asks how such news can hold, stating the reproductive improbability within the announcement.
The messengers affirm the glad tidings as true and tell him not to despair, making hope in divine giving the answer to bodily improbability.
The direction of the path is said to belong to God while some ways deviate, closely paralleling the divine stance of 'upon Us is guidance' that the section also hears as leading to arrival.
The night and day are two signs: the night-sign is effaced and the day-sign made visible so people may seek bounty and reckon time, elaborating cover, disclosure, provision, and measure.
One man reminds another that God created him from dust, then a drop, then fashioned him as a man, another compact route from generative matter to embodied human form.
After Mary's labor she is told to eat, drink, and be comforted, completing the preceding water-and-dates scene as provision for the mother after difficult birth.
Creation of the human from an extract of clay supplies the first stage of the sequence continued by the womb lodging in 23:13 and embryonic formation in 23:14.
Female and male sexual offenders receive the same stated punishment, a legal boundary around sexual approach in which sex does not alter accountability.
Corrupt and good women and men are paired by moral description, shifting the decisive correspondence between the sexes from sex itself to character.
The prayer for spouses and offspring as a comfort to the eyes presents family as a requested gift and sight as delight rather than the darkened face of unwanted birth.
Night becomes a sign when day is stripped from it and people are left in darkness, a vivid reversal of the section's daylight unveiling.
This ayah identifies the surrounding offspring-claim as the speakers' fabrication, clarifying that the daughter-son questions expose their lie rather than rank either sex.
The explicit claim that God begot is declared false, supplying the theological boundary behind 37:149-153 between created sexual generation and the Creator.
Believing men and believing women share admission to gardens and forgiveness, another outcome determined by faith rather than sex.
Hypocritical and associating men and women likewise share judgment for their corrupt stance, completing 48:5's demonstration that the moral divide crosses both sexes.
Hypocritical men and women together ask the believers to wait so they can take from their light, extending 57:12's male-female light scene with a moral, rather than sexual, division.
The wives of Noah and Lot are not saved by marriage to righteous men, showing that spousal union does not determine a woman's moral end.
Pharaoh's believing wife asks God for a house in the Garden, showing conversely that marriage to a corrupt man does not determine a woman's moral end.
Sleep is made repose between creation in pairs and night as garment, adding bodily rest to the passage's pair-cover-day sequence.
Pharaoh's claim to be the lord most high is the false human seizure of the height-title that the section reserves for God.

The production of humanity from one soul followed by a place of settlement and a repository may echo generation and hidden keeping, although the two locations admit interpretations broader than the womb.
